item.content:encoded:
The Takemi Program in International Health at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health is accepting applications for its 2027–2028 fellowship year, offering mid-career health professionals and researchers an opportunity to spend an academic year at Harvard developing an independent research project, strengthening their research capacity, and advancing their leadership in international health.

The program is particularly relevant to professionals working on health systems, global health, health policy, health financing, disease prevention and control, health equity, public health, and other challenges involving the mobilization and allocation of limited resources for better health outcomes.

Applications for the 2027–2028 program are currently open, and the official deadline is December 31, 2026, at midnight EST (USA).

About the Harvard Takemi Program in International Health

The Takemi Program in International Health is an interdisciplinary research and leadership program at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.

The program brings a small group of mid-career health professionals and scholars to Harvard for an academic year to conduct focused research and develop their capacity for research and leadership.

The program’s central focus is on understanding how limited resources can be mobilized, allocated, and managed to improve health and health systems. Its research has a strong emphasis on practical health challenges, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.

Since its establishment in 1983, the program has developed a large international network of Takemi Fellows. Harvard currently reports that more than 330 fellows from more than 60 countries have participated in the program.

The program was named after Dr. Taro Takemi, a distinguished Japanese physician-scientist who served as president of the Japan Medical Association for more than two decades.

What Is the Takemi Fellowship?

The Takemi Program is designed for mid-career researchers and health professionals who have already developed substantial professional and research experience and want to dedicate an academic year to advancing a specific research project.

Unlike a conventional degree program, the Takemi Program is centered on an individual research project.

Each fellow works with a Harvard faculty advisor and uses the fellowship year to:

  • Develop and conduct a focused research project
  • Analyze existing data
  • Strengthen research methodology
  • Engage with Harvard faculty and researchers
  • Participate in weekly academic seminars
  • Present research findings and receive feedback
  • Develop a publication-quality research paper
  • Strengthen leadership capacity
  • Build international professional networks
  • Explore relevant Harvard coursework and academic resources

The program is conducted in person in Boston and does not offer a remote fellowship option.

Who Is the Takemi Program Designed For?

The program is primarily intended for mid-career health professionals and researchers.

Applicants should not view this as a typical early-career fellowship or a postgraduate degree scholarship. Harvard specifically describes the program as being for professionals and researchers who already have an advanced degree, significant work and research experience, publications, and demonstrated leadership potential.

Potential applicants may come from areas such as:

  • Public health
  • Medicine
  • Pharmacy
  • Nursing
  • Epidemiology
  • Health economics
  • Health policy
  • Health systems
  • Global health
  • Health administration
  • Nutrition
  • Health financing
  • Disease prevention and control
  • Implementation science
  • Health services research
  • Social and behavioral sciences
  • Other fields relevant to international health

The most important consideration is not simply the applicant’s professional title. The proposed research should fit the program’s broader focus on improving health and health systems through better use of resources, stronger policies, and evidence-based interventions.

What Makes the Takemi Program Different?

The Takemi Program is particularly valuable because it provides fellows with something that can be difficult to obtain while working full-time: dedicated time and an academic environment to focus intensively on research.

Harvard describes the program as providing fellows with the space, time, and flexibility to enhance their research and leadership capacity.

Rather than requiring fellows to complete a conventional curriculum, the program allows them to concentrate on a research project that is relevant to their professional work and future contribution to health policy or practice.

This makes the program especially relevant for professionals who already have a research question, access to data, and a clear idea of how their research could contribute to improving health systems or policy.

Research Focus of the Takemi Program

The program’s research emphasis is broad but strongly connected to real-world international health challenges.

Research can examine questions related to:

Health Systems

Projects may investigate how health systems are organized, financed, managed, or improved.

Health Policy

Applicants may explore policies affecting health outcomes, healthcare delivery, access, equity, financing, or population health.

Health Resource Allocation

A central theme of the program is understanding how scarce resources can be allocated more effectively to achieve better health outcomes.

Disease Prevention and Control

Research may focus on strategies for preventing, controlling, or managing important diseases and health threats.

Health Promotion

Projects may examine interventions designed to improve population health and encourage healthier behaviors.

Global Health

The program is particularly interested in major health challenges affecting low- and middle-income countries and approaches that can produce practical improvements.

Health Equity

Research examining inequalities, access to healthcare, marginalized populations, and equitable distribution of health resources may also fit within the program’s broader research priorities.

Harvard states that Takemi research has a strong practical emphasis and that projects should be closely connected to action and to the fellow’s work after returning home.

A Critical Requirement: Your Data Must Already Be Available

One of the most important requirements for prospective applicants is that their research project must be ready for analysis before the fellowship begins.

Takemi does not support active data collection during the fellowship.

Harvard explicitly states that fellows are expected to conduct their research using data they bring with them and that having the necessary data collected before the program begins is mandatory.

This means applicants should not propose a research project that depends on spending the fellowship year conducting extensive surveys, recruiting participants, collecting laboratory samples, or otherwise gathering primary data.

Instead, a strong proposal should demonstrate that:

  1. The research question has already been defined.
  2. The necessary data are available.
  3. The applicant has access to the data.
  4. The data are sufficiently prepared for analysis.
  5. The proposed methodology can realistically be implemented during the fellowship year.
  6. The research can result in a publication-quality paper.

This requirement is particularly important when designing the research proposal.

Faculty Supervision and Research Mentorship

Each selected fellow is matched with a Harvard faculty advisor based on the fellow’s background and proposed research.

Applicants do not need to independently secure a Harvard faculty supervisor before applying.

Harvard explains that fellows are matched with faculty mentors after selection based on their background and proposed research.

The faculty advisor provides guidance and feedback throughout the research process.

Fellows also receive guidance from the Takemi Program leadership and benefit from interactions with other fellows and the broader Harvard community.

Weekly Takemi Seminar Series

An important component of the program is the weekly Takemi Seminar Series.

The seminars expose fellows to a broad range of research topics, methodologies, and perspectives through presentations by Harvard faculty and distinguished visiting scholars.

The seminars also create opportunities for discussion and intellectual exchange between fellows, faculty, and invited speakers.

This means the fellowship is not simply an individual research residency. Fellows become part of an academic community where they can receive feedback, exchange ideas, and learn from researchers working on different international health challenges.

Research Presentations During the Fellowship

Takemi Fellows are expected to present their research progress during the fellowship.

According to Harvard, fellows participate in:

  • Preliminary presentations
  • Mid-year presentations
  • Final presentations
  • Final academic poster presentation

These presentations provide opportunities for fellows to receive feedback from faculty advisors and peers as they develop their research.

By the end of the fellowship, fellows are expected to produce a final paper of publishable quality and a research poster.

Opportunity to Audit Harvard Courses

Although the Takemi Program is primarily a research fellowship, fellows may also have opportunities to audit classes at Harvard Chan School.

They are also encouraged to attend Harvard Chan seminars and other academic events.

This can allow fellows to supplement their research experience with additional academic exposure based on their professional and research interests.

Fellowship Duration

The Takemi Program is a full academic-year fellowship.

Harvard states that the fellowship runs from:

August 1 through June 30

Fellows are expected to arrive before the program orientation, which takes place in late August. The certificate ceremony is generally held in early May.

Applicants should therefore plan for a substantial period of residence in Boston rather than treating the fellowship as a short-term visiting researcher position.

What Applicants Need to Submit

The application includes several components designed to assess the applicant’s academic background, professional experience, research capacity, motivation, and leadership potential.

The application requires the following:

1. Eligibility Questionnaire

Applicants must complete the program’s eligibility questionnaire.

This helps establish whether the applicant meets the fundamental requirements for consideration.

2. Proof of English Language Proficiency

Applicants must provide evidence of English proficiency.

The application accepts:

  • TOEFL
  • IELTS

Applicants who attended a university where English was the language of instruction may submit a copy of their transcript as evidence, according to the application instructions provided.

3. Statement of Interest

The Statement of Interest is an important component of the application.

Applicants should explain:

  • Why they are interested in the Takemi Program
  • Why the fellowship is important at this stage of their career
  • How the program will contribute to their professional development
  • What they can contribute to the Takemi community
  • Why they believe they would succeed in the program
  • What they hope to gain from the fellowship
  • What they plan to do after completing the program

A strong statement should connect the applicant’s past experience, current research interests, Takemi fellowship objectives, and future professional plans.

4. Basic Information

Applicants will provide standard personal and application information through the online application portal.

5. Education and Professional Experience

Applicants must provide information about their academic and professional background.

This section allows the program to understand the applicant’s progression and experience in relation to the fellowship.

6. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must upload a current CV in PDF format.

The CV should clearly present relevant:

  • Academic qualifications
  • Professional experience
  • Research experience
  • Publications
  • Leadership roles
  • Awards and recognition
  • Relevant projects
  • Professional activities

Because the Takemi Program is designed for mid-career professionals, the CV should clearly demonstrate the applicant’s professional trajectory and research accomplishments.

7. Research Proposal

The research proposal is arguably one of the most important components of the application.

Applicants must submit a research proposal of no more than five pages, excluding the title page and references.

The proposal should be:

  • Single-spaced
  • 12-point Times New Roman
  • Submitted as a PDF

The proposal should include the following sections.

Title Page

The title page should clearly identify the proposed research project.

Summary of the Proposed Project

The summary should provide a concise overview of the research, including:

  • The central research problem
  • Specific aims and objectives
  • Potential significance of the research

The application guidance suggests approximately half a page for this section.

Specific Aims

Applicants should clearly explain what the research intends to accomplish.

The suggested length is approximately half a page to one page.

Background and Significance

This section should establish:

  • What is already known
  • What problem remains
  • Why the problem matters
  • Why the proposed research is important
  • How the project contributes to existing knowledge

Data Sources

Applicants should identify the data that will be used.

This is particularly important because the program requires the necessary data to already be collected before the fellowship begins.

Research Design and Methods

This section should explain how the research will be conducted.

Applicants should clearly describe:

  • Research design
  • Analytical approach
  • Variables or measures
  • Methods
  • Data analysis
  • Any relevant methodological considerations

The application guidance suggests approximately two pages for this section.

References

The proposal should conclude with relevant references.

8. Publication List

Applicants must provide a list of their publications.

This requirement reflects the program’s emphasis on applicants who already have demonstrated research experience and scholarly output.

Applicants should ensure that the publication list is accurate, clearly organized, and consistent with the CV.

9. Published Document in English

Applicants must provide a document published in English.

This gives the selection committee an opportunity to assess the applicant’s ability to communicate scholarly work in English.

10. Three References

Applicants must provide the names and contact information of three referees.

After the application is submitted, referees receive an automated request to submit their references to the Takemi Program.

Applicants should therefore choose referees who can provide meaningful evidence of their:

  • Research ability
  • Professional experience
  • Leadership potential
  • Academic development
  • Contribution to health systems or policy
  • Capacity to benefit from the fellowship

Who Is Eligible for the Takemi Program?

Harvard’s current application guidance states that applicants should be mid-career researchers and professionals who have:

  • Completed an advanced degree
  • Significant work experience
  • Significant research experience
  • Publications in internationally recognized journals
  • Demonstrated potential for leadership in their home countries
  • Appropriate preparation to benefit from the program
  • Strong English-language ability

The program is primarily designed for people who are already established in their professional careers rather than recent graduates.

Is the Takemi Program Open to International Applicants?

Yes.

The Takemi Program is explicitly international and brings together professionals and researchers from around the world.

Harvard’s historical fellowship network includes fellows from countries across:

  • Africa
  • Asia
  • Europe
  • The Middle East
  • North America
  • South America
  • Other regions

Harvard describes the program as having a particular emphasis on fellows from low- and middle-income countries.

Therefore, the opportunity is not restricted to U.S. citizens or residents.

Professionals from eligible countries around the world can apply if they meet the program’s academic, professional, research, and leadership requirements.

Is There a Race or Ethnicity Requirement?

The program does not specify a racial or ethnic eligibility restriction.

Its emphasis is instead on professional background, research experience, leadership potential, English proficiency, and the relevance and quality of the proposed research.

Harvard also states that the Takemi Program welcomes research examining issues related to racism, discrimination, marginalization, structural inequality, and other related issues when relevant to international health research.

Preference for Low- and Middle-Income Countries

The Takemi Program has a longstanding commitment to strengthening research and leadership capacity among professionals from low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).

Harvard states that the program has historically focused on building the capacity of mid-career researchers from LMICs and that most Takemi Fellows have focused their work on LMIC-related challenges.

This makes the program particularly relevant for professionals whose work addresses health challenges in developing and emerging economies.

Financial Support and Funding

Applicants should pay close attention to funding arrangements.

The Takemi Program states that incoming fellows are generally responsible for securing funding to support their fellowship year. Boston is an expensive city, and Harvard encourages accepted candidates to plan carefully for the cost of living and other expenses.

However, limited funding mechanisms are available.

For example, Harvard reports that a contribution from the Japan Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association (JPMA) provides partial financial support for up to two fellows from low-income countries each year. Candidates can indicate their interest in this support during the application process.

Importantly, applicants should not assume that the Takemi fellowship automatically provides full funding for the entire year.

Accepted applicants may need to secure funding through other sources, such as:

  • Employer or professional development funding
  • Government funding
  • Research grants
  • International fellowships
  • Fulbright funding
  • Other external funding sources

Harvard provides information about potential external funding sources for incoming fellows.

Application Deadline

The deadline for the 2027–2028 Takemi Program in International Health is:

December 31, 2026

Applications must be submitted by midnight EST (USA) on December 31, 2026.

Applicants should avoid waiting until the final day because the application includes multiple documents, a research proposal, English-language documentation, publications, and three references.

Click HERE to read more and apply.

Conclusion

The Harvard Takemi Program in International Health 2027–2028 represents a significant opportunity for experienced health professionals and researchers seeking dedicated time to conduct high-quality research, strengthen their leadership capacity, and contribute to better health policies and systems.

The program is particularly relevant to mid-career professionals with advanced degrees, substantial research and professional experience, international publications, and demonstrated leadership potential. Its strong emphasis on practical research makes it especially suitable for applicants whose work addresses health challenges in low- and middle-income countries.

The program is also international rather than restricted to U.S. applicants, making it potentially relevant to qualified health professionals and researchers across Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Middle East, Europe, and other regions. Harvard’s fellowship network demonstrates its longstanding international reach.

The application deadline is December 31, 2026, at midnight EST (USA). Applicants should begin preparing well in advance because the application requires a research proposal, statement of interest, CV, publication list, English-language documentation, writing sample, and three references.

item.content:encoded:
NASA has opened applications for its Spring 2027 Office of STEM Engagement (OSTEM) Internship Program, offering students the opportunity to gain hands-on experience by contributing to real NASA projects and working alongside NASA professionals.

For students interested in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, space exploration, aeronautics, research, communications, business, and other fields relevant to NASA’s mission, the OSTEM program can provide valuable practical experience, professional development, and exposure to one of the world’s leading space and science organizations.

The application deadline for the Spring 2027 NASA OSTEM Internships is September 14, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time.

Applicants should therefore review available opportunities, confirm their eligibility, prepare their application materials, and submit their applications before the deadline.

About the NASA OSTEM Internship Program

NASA’s Office of STEM Engagement (OSTEM) runs internship opportunities designed to give students practical experience connected to NASA’s missions.

According to NASA, the OSTEM program provides students with short-term, hands-on opportunities to work on real NASA projects. Interns can develop technical and professional skills while receiving guidance and mentorship from NASA personnel.

NASA provides more than 2,000 students annually with opportunities through its OSTEM internship program.

The program is therefore more than a conventional academic internship. Selected students have the opportunity to gain experience in a professional environment and contribute to projects connected to NASA’s broader work in science, technology, aeronautics, and space exploration.

What Is the Spring 2027 NASA OSTEM Internship?

The Spring 2027 OSTEM internship is part of NASA’s annual internship cycle.

NASA operates three major OSTEM internship sessions each year:

  • Spring
  • Summer
  • Fall

For the Spring 2027 cycle, applications must be submitted by September 14, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. ET.

The spring and fall OSTEM internships generally run for approximately 15 weeks, while summer internships generally last around 10 weeks.

What Do NASA OSTEM Interns Do?

NASA OSTEM interns work on projects that contribute to the agency’s mission.

Depending on the specific internship, responsibilities can vary considerably. NASA offers opportunities across a broad range of academic and professional disciplines.

Interns may have the opportunity to:

  • Work on real NASA projects
  • Conduct research and analysis
  • Support scientific or engineering activities
  • Develop technical solutions
  • Analyze data
  • Assist with communications and outreach
  • Contribute to technology development
  • Work with NASA scientists, engineers, researchers, and other professionals
  • Develop professional and workplace skills
  • Gain practical experience related to their academic field
  • Participate in a professional NASA work environment

Importantly, NASA states that its internship opportunities are not limited exclusively to STEM majors. NASA also offers opportunities for students from non-STEM disciplines, depending on the available projects and NASA’s workforce needs.

This means students should not automatically assume that they are ineligible simply because their degree is not in engineering, physics, computer science, or another traditional STEM discipline.

Key Benefits of a NASA OSTEM Internship

A NASA internship can provide several important benefits for students seeking to build their academic and professional careers.

1. Gain Hands-On Professional Experience

One of the major advantages of the OSTEM program is the opportunity to move beyond classroom learning.

Interns can work on projects and activities that provide practical experience and help them understand how their academic knowledge can be applied in a professional environment.

2. Work on Real NASA Projects

OSTEM internships are designed around actual NASA projects rather than purely theoretical assignments.

Students can contribute to work related to NASA’s broader mission in areas such as science, technology, aeronautics, and space exploration.

3. Learn From NASA Professionals

Interns have the opportunity to work with NASA experts and mentors.

This can expose students to professional approaches to:

  • Research
  • Problem-solving
  • Project management
  • Technical work
  • Communication
  • Collaboration
  • Innovation

4. Strengthen Your Resume

Having hands-on experience with NASA can be a valuable addition to a student’s academic and professional profile.

The experience can demonstrate exposure to:

  • Professional project environments
  • Research or technical work
  • Team collaboration
  • Problem-solving
  • Innovation
  • Mission-oriented work

Students can subsequently use the experience when applying for graduate programmes, scholarships, research opportunities, jobs, and other internships.

5. Develop Technical and Professional Skills

NASA describes OSTEM internships as opportunities to build both technical skills and career readiness.

Depending on the project, students may develop skills related to their discipline while also strengthening transferable skills such as communication, teamwork, organization, critical thinking, and professional problem-solving.

6. Explore Careers at NASA

An OSTEM internship can also help students understand what it is like to work within NASA and explore potential career paths.

For students interested in eventually pursuing careers in aerospace, science, engineering, research, technology, communications, administration, or other NASA-related fields, an internship can provide useful exposure to the organization.

Who Can Apply for the NASA OSTEM Internship?

NASA’s current eligibility requirements specify that OSTEM candidates must meet several requirements.

Applicants must:

  • Be a U.S. citizen
  • Be at least 16 years old at the time of application
  • Have a minimum 3.0 cumulative GPA on a 4.0 scale
  • Be a full-time or part-time college student, from undergraduate through graduate level
  • Be enrolled in a degree-granting programme at a U.S. Department of Education-accredited college or university
  • Be studying in a course of study aligned with NASA’s needs

NASA also indicates that educators who are enrolled as students can be eligible to apply.

Students who have recently graduated may also be eligible for internships taking place during the three internship sessions immediately following their graduation, subject to NASA’s eligibility requirements.

Do You Need to Study a STEM Subject?

Not necessarily.

The name “Office of STEM Engagement” might lead some applicants to believe that only STEM students can apply. However, NASA explicitly states that it offers internships for non-STEM majors as well.

The key consideration is whether the applicant’s academic programme and qualifications align with the requirements of the particular internship opportunity.

Therefore, students from fields outside traditional STEM disciplines should review the individual project descriptions rather than automatically ruling themselves out.

How Long Is the NASA OSTEM Internship?

The length of the internship depends on the session.

NASA’s current programme information indicates:

  • Spring: approximately 15 weeks
  • Summer: approximately 10 weeks
  • Fall: approximately 15 weeks

The exact dates and working arrangements can vary according to the specific internship project.

Is the NASA OSTEM Internship Paid?

Yes.

NASA describes OSTEM internships as paid internships.

This makes the opportunity particularly attractive to students who want to gain high-level professional experience while receiving financial compensation during the internship.

Applicants should review the specific opportunity listing for the details applicable to the position they are applying for.

Is the NASA Internship Available to International Students?

This is an important point for international applicants.

For the standard NASA OSTEM Internship Program, NASA’s current eligibility requirements state that applicants must be U.S. citizens.

Therefore, students living in countries such as Ethiopia, Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana, South Africa, India, the United Kingdom, Canada, or other countries generally cannot apply for the standard Spring 2027 OSTEM internship solely on the basis of being international students.

NASA previously operated international internship arrangements through its International Internship (I²) programme. However, NASA’s current international internship page states that the International Internship (I²) programme is not being offered at this time.

Students who are not U.S. citizens should therefore carefully distinguish the standard OSTEM programme from any separate NASA international opportunities that may become available in the future.

Important Citizenship Requirement

The citizenship requirement is particularly important because some online posts about NASA internships may make the opportunity appear open to students worldwide.

For the current OSTEM programme, NASA explicitly states:

U.S. citizenship is required.

International students should not assume that studying at a U.S. university automatically makes them eligible for OSTEM. The official eligibility requirement is U.S. citizenship.

What Academic Level Is Eligible?

NASA’s OSTEM programme is intended for students at multiple levels of higher education.

Eligible students can include:

  • Undergraduate students
  • Graduate students
  • Other college-level students who meet NASA’s requirements

The programme requires applicants to be enrolled in an eligible degree-granting programme at a U.S.-accredited institution.

The minimum age is 16 years old at the time of application.

GPA Requirement

Applicants must have a minimum cumulative GPA of:

3.0 out of 4.0

This is an important eligibility requirement and should be checked before submitting an application.

Applicants should also review the requirements listed on each individual internship opportunity because individual projects may have additional qualifications or preferences.

Application Deadline for NASA Spring 2027 Internships

The most important date for students interested in this opportunity is:

September 14, 2026

The official NASA internship page specifies that applications for the Spring 2027 OSTEM session close at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on September 14, 2026.

Applicants should not wait until the final hours to submit their applications.

Technical problems, incomplete information, missing documents, or last-minute application issues can create unnecessary risks.

How to Apply for the NASA Spring 2027 OSTEM Internship

Applicants should begin by reviewing the available NASA OSTEM internship opportunities and identifying projects that match their academic background, interests, skills, and career goals.

The general process is:

Step 1: Review the Available Opportunities

Look through the NASA OSTEM internship listings and identify projects that match your interests and qualifications.

Step 2: Check the Eligibility Requirements

Before spending significant time on an application, confirm that you meet the basic requirements, including:

  • U.S. citizenship
  • Minimum age
  • GPA
  • Student status
  • Educational institution requirements
  • Academic field requirements

Step 3: Identify the Best-Fit Projects

Do not simply apply randomly.

Review the project description and consider:

  • What skills are requested?
  • What academic background is preferred?
  • What responsibilities are involved?
  • What technical or professional experience would be useful?
  • How does the project relate to your career goals?

Step 4: Prepare Your Application

Make sure your application accurately communicates your:

  • Academic background
  • Relevant experience
  • Skills
  • Research interests
  • Career objectives
  • Relevant projects
  • Leadership or extracurricular activities

Step 5: Submit Before the Deadline

Applications for Spring 2027 must be submitted by:

September 14, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. ET.

Applicants should allow sufficient time to complete and review their application before the deadline.

A Note for International Applicants

International students should pay particular attention to the citizenship requirement before investing time in an OSTEM application.

The current NASA OSTEM requirements state that candidates must be U.S. citizens.

NASA’s International Internship programme page also currently states that the International Internship (I²) programme is not being offered at this time.

NASA does, however, encourage international students to explore certain NASA student challenges and citizen science projects.

Therefore, international students should monitor NASA’s official pages for other opportunities rather than assuming that the Spring 2027 OSTEM programme is open internationally.

Click HERE to read more and apply.

Conclusion

The NASA Spring 2027 OSTEM Internship Program provides eligible students with an opportunity to gain paid, hands-on experience while contributing to projects connected to NASA’s mission.

The programme is designed for students at different stages of higher education and can accommodate a broad range of academic disciplines, including some non-STEM fields. Interns can develop technical and professional skills, gain practical workplace experience, work with NASA professionals, and strengthen their career readiness.

However, applicants should pay close attention to the eligibility requirements. The current OSTEM programme requires applicants to be U.S. citizens, at least 16 years old, enrolled in an eligible programme at a U.S.-accredited institution, and have a minimum 3.0 GPA.

The deadline for the Spring 2027 NASA OSTEM Internship is September 14, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time.

Students who meet the requirements should begin reviewing the available opportunities and preparing their applications as early as possible.

About the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria

The Global Fund is an international financing partnership dedicated to accelerating progress against HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria while supporting stronger and more resilient health systems.

Rather than directly implementing most country programs itself, the Global Fund finances programs that are implemented through its partners and Principal Recipients. This distinction is important when reviewing its business opportunities.

The organization’s Business & Consultancy Opportunities page primarily covers procurement undertaken by the Global Fund itself, particularly requirements of its Secretariat. Principal Recipients administering Global Fund grants may conduct their own procurement processes separately in accordance with applicable grant requirements.

The Global Fund’s procurement activities are intended to support its organizational operations while helping ensure that resources ultimately contribute to effective global health interventions.

What Are Global Fund Business and Consultancy Opportunities?

The opportunities published through the platform are essentially competitive procurement exercises.

Depending on the requirement, the Global Fund may seek proposals from:

  • Individual consultants
  • Consultancy firms
  • Professional service providers
  • Companies
  • Contractors
  • Suppliers
  • Manufacturers
  • Technical organizations
  • Research organizations
  • Specialist agencies
  • Procurement service providers
  • Other qualified entities

The Global Fund’s Procurement Policy defines a supplier broadly as an external entity that may include an organization, individual contractor or service provider supplying goods, services or other support.

Consequently, applicants should not assume that every opportunity is intended for an individual consultant. Some tenders may require established companies or organizations capable of delivering substantial contracts.

What Types of Opportunities May Be Available?

The exact opportunities change throughout the year.

Potential procurement areas can include professional and technical services associated with the Global Fund’s operations and mission.

Depending on organizational requirements, opportunities may potentially cover areas such as:

  • Global health consulting
  • HIV-related technical services
  • Tuberculosis programs and expertise
  • Malaria-related technical services
  • Health-system strengthening
  • Procurement and supply-chain services
  • Public-health analysis
  • Data and analytics
  • Monitoring and evaluation
  • Independent evaluation
  • Research
  • Strategy development
  • Organizational consulting
  • Finance and accounting services
  • Audit and assurance
  • Risk management
  • Information technology
  • Digital systems
  • Communications
  • Knowledge management
  • Human resources consulting
  • Legal or regulatory support
  • Program management
  • Project management
  • Logistics
  • Procurement of goods
  • Health-product procurement
  • Pharmaceutical products
  • Diagnostic products
  • Other specialized technical or operational services

Actual eligibility and technical requirements are determined separately for each solicitation.

Global Fund Consulting Opportunities

Consultancy assignments represent an important component of the Global Fund’s external contracting activities.

The Global Fund’s careers information confirms that it engages both individual consultants and consultancy firms, with relevant opportunities published through the Business & Consultancy Opportunities section.

These assignments should not be confused with permanent employment vacancies.

Permanent and fixed-term staff vacancies generally appear through the Global Fund’s separate careers system, while consulting and supplier procurements are normally handled as contracting opportunities.

Consultants may therefore be engaged to deliver specific outputs, technical expertise, analysis, assessments, evaluations or other professional services under contractual terms defined in the relevant solicitation.

Global Fund Procurement Opportunities for Suppliers

Companies interested in doing business with the Global Fund should understand that procurement is governed by formal institutional rules.

The Global Fund states that it seeks value for money in the procurement of goods and services and publishes tenders as part of a transparent procurement process.

Its Procurement Policy applies to several areas, including:

  1. Procurement of health products and related services through the Pooled Procurement Mechanism.
  2. Procurement of goods and services financed through Global Fund operating expenses.
  3. Certain other procurements financed through approved investments or funds.
  4. Procurement of Local Fund Agent services.

This means the procurement framework covers both operational requirements and major elements of the organization’s health-product supply system.

Open Competition Is the Standard Procurement Approach

One of the most important aspects for prospective bidders is the Global Fund’s emphasis on competitive procurement.

Its Procurement Policy states that procurement should generally be based on effective competition and identifies open competition as the organization’s standard procurement method.

Effective competition may involve:

  • Publicly advertising procurement opportunities;
  • Inviting a sufficient number of prospective suppliers;
  • Ensuring bidders compete under equivalent conditions;
  • Receiving sufficient independent offers; and
  • Evaluating proposals against established requirements.

This approach is intended to provide a transparent and competitive environment for qualified suppliers.

Core Global Fund Procurement Principles

Prospective applicants should understand the principles against which Global Fund procurement is managed.

1. Value for Money

Procurement decisions are not necessarily based solely on selecting the lowest-priced offer.

The Global Fund defines value for money by considering the relationship among:

  • Price
  • Quality
  • Performance
  • Total cost of ownership
  • Technical suitability
  • Delivery requirements
  • Organizational capability

Environmental, social, sustainability and risk considerations may also be incorporated where relevant.

A bidder should therefore ensure that its proposal demonstrates overall value rather than simply offering a low financial price.

2. Effective Competition

Competitive procurement is intended to ensure multiple qualified suppliers have a fair opportunity to participate.

The organization seeks an adequate competitive environment and normally uses open competition as its standard approach.

3. Fairness, Impartiality and Integrity

The Global Fund requires bidders to be treated equally and proposals to be evaluated objectively against predetermined criteria.

Its Procurement Policy specifically emphasizes avoiding actual, potential or perceived conflicts of interest.

4. Client-Centered Procurement

Procurement is also expected to meet the requirements of the internal Global Fund unit requesting the goods or services.

This means suppliers must closely understand the technical specifications and intended outcomes of each tender.

5. Sustainable Procurement

The Global Fund explicitly incorporates sustainability into its procurement framework.

Its policy states that sustainable procurement seeks to:

  • Reduce environmental impacts across supply chains;
  • Support fair and humane working conditions;
  • Promote social progress;
  • Support economic development; and
  • Contribute to the long-term well-being of communities.

6. Best Interests of the Global Fund

Procurement must ultimately support the organization’s mission, protect its assets and ensure responsible stewardship of its resources.

Ethical Requirements for Global Fund Suppliers

Ethical compliance is a major requirement for companies and consultants seeking contracts with the organization.

The Global Fund’s Code of Conduct for Suppliers applies broadly to bidders, suppliers, agents, intermediaries, consultants and contractors, as well as relevant representatives, employees, subcontractors and affiliates.

Suppliers are expected to participate in procurement processes honestly, fairly, transparently and accountably.

The organization prohibits practices including:

  • Corruption
  • Fraud
  • Collusion
  • Anti-competitive practices
  • Coercion
  • Misrepresentation
  • Improper payments
  • Undisclosed commissions
  • Other unethical procurement practices

Applicants should therefore ensure that every statement, qualification, reference, financial proposal and declaration contained in their bid is accurate.

Compliance With Laws

Suppliers and their representatives are required to comply with applicable laws and regulations in the countries where they conduct business, as well as relevant Global Fund rules and policies.

The Code of Conduct also includes provisions concerning matters such as:

  • Anti-corruption
  • Anti-money laundering
  • Fair competition
  • Responsible use of Global Fund resources
  • Disclosure of conflicts
  • Human rights
  • Labor standards
  • Environmental responsibilities
  • Child protection
  • Protection from sexual exploitation and abuse and sexual harassment

These requirements should be treated as substantive contractual obligations rather than formalities.

Record-Keeping and Audit Requirements

Companies that obtain Global Fund-financed contracts should also be prepared for accountability and audit requirements.

The Supplier Code of Conduct requires suppliers to maintain appropriate and complete financial and business records associated with Global Fund-financed contracts for at least five years after the final payment under the contract.

Suppliers are also expected to cooperate with the Global Fund, including its Office of the Inspector General, where access to relevant records, documents or personnel is reasonably requested.

This requirement is particularly relevant to larger consulting firms, contractors and suppliers managing financially significant contracts.

Conflicts of Interest

Potential suppliers must pay close attention to conflict-of-interest requirements.

The procurement framework seeks to ensure objective evaluation and prevent circumstances where a bidder could obtain an improper competitive advantage.

Suppliers should disclose relevant relationships or situations where required and carefully review the specific tender documentation before submitting their proposal.

Failure to properly address conflicts may jeopardize a bid or contract.

Can Suppliers Use the Global Fund Name or Logo?

Winning a Global Fund contract does not automatically authorize a supplier to use the organization’s name or logo for advertising.

The Supplier Code states that suppliers may not, without prior written consent, use the Global Fund’s name or logo in publicity or advertising, represent a business relationship as an endorsement of their products or services, or make statements on behalf of the Global Fund.

Companies should therefore obtain appropriate authorization before publicly promoting a contractual relationship.

Health Product Procurement Opportunities

The Global Fund is also a major procurer of medicines and health products.

Its Pooled Procurement Mechanism (PPM) aggregates orders from participating grant implementers to obtain competitive prices and delivery conditions from manufacturers and suppliers.

In 2025, the mechanism handled approximately US$1.02 billion in orders for implementing partners in 81 countries.

Products available through the mechanism include categories such as:

  • Antiretroviral medicines
  • Antimalarial medicines
  • Other essential medicines
  • Insecticide-treated mosquito nets
  • Viral load tests
  • Rapid diagnostic tests

Regular tenders for medicines and diagnostic products may also appear through the Business & Consultancy Opportunities section.

Important Information for Health Product Suppliers

Companies interested specifically in supplying medicines or health products should not rely exclusively on the general tender page.

The Global Fund advises potential health-product suppliers to:

  1. Review its Procurement Policy.
  2. Understand quality-assurance requirements applicable to their products.
  3. Review relevant procurement and purchasing information.
  4. Understand the Pooled Procurement Mechanism and wambo.org.
  5. Review the Code of Conduct for Suppliers.
  6. Review applicable procurement regulations.

The organization does not maintain a general list of automatically preselected suppliers for implementing partners.

Manufacturers must therefore satisfy the particular regulatory, quality and procurement conditions applicable to their products.

What Documents Should Applicants Read Before Applying?

The Global Fund explicitly advises prospective bidders to review key procurement documentation before submitting a proposal.

Important documents include:

  • Procurement Policy
  • Code of Conduct for Suppliers
  • Terms and Conditions for the Purchase of Goods and Services
  • Privacy Statement for the Global Fund Procurement Process
  • Travel Guidelines for Contractors

Applicants should not treat these documents as optional background reading.

They can establish important conditions relating to:

  • Ethical conduct
  • Contract administration
  • Financial arrangements
  • Confidentiality
  • Travel
  • Compliance
  • Reporting
  • Supplier obligations
  • Legal liability

Tender-specific conditions may supplement these general rules.

How to Apply for Global Fund Business and Consultancy Opportunities

The application procedure is not identical for every procurement.

The official Business & Consultancy Opportunities page directs applicants to the Global Fund’s Open Tenders platform.

Each individual solicitation contains its own:

  • Tender description
  • Terms of reference or specifications
  • Eligibility requirements
  • Required qualifications
  • Submission procedure
  • Technical documentation
  • Financial requirements
  • Deadline
  • Contact or clarification procedure

Applicants should therefore first identify a tender that matches their qualifications and carefully review the complete tender package before preparing a proposal.

View Global Fund Business & Consultancy Opportunities

Preparing a Competitive Proposal

Although tender requirements vary, applicants should generally prepare to demonstrate why they are technically and commercially capable of delivering the requested work.

A strong proposal may need to address areas such as:

Understanding of the Assignment

Demonstrate a clear understanding of:

  • The Global Fund’s requirements
  • Expected outputs
  • Relevant technical issues
  • Contract objectives
  • Deliverables

Technical Approach

Where required, explain:

  • Proposed methodology
  • Implementation approach
  • Work plan
  • Quality-assurance arrangements
  • Risk management
  • Project governance
  • Reporting arrangements

Relevant Experience

Applicants may need to demonstrate previous experience delivering similar assignments.

Evidence could include:

  • Comparable contracts
  • Client references
  • Case studies
  • Project summaries
  • Past performance
  • Demonstrated international experience

Personnel

Consultancy tenders may require CVs of proposed experts.

Applicants should ensure that each proposed team member clearly satisfies any mandatory:

  • Education requirements
  • Professional qualifications
  • Years of experience
  • Technical competencies
  • Language requirements

Financial Proposal

Price should be realistic and consistent with the technical methodology.

Because Global Fund procurement evaluates overall value for money rather than price alone, applicants should avoid compromising technical quality merely to submit the lowest possible price.

Evaluation of Proposals

The exact scoring methodology will be provided in the individual tender documentation.

However, the Global Fund’s overarching Procurement Policy permits consideration of:

  • Technical factors
  • Commercial factors
  • Organizational factors
  • Pricing
  • Environmental factors
  • Social considerations
  • Sustainability
  • Risk
  • Appropriate due diligence

Applicants should therefore respond directly to every evaluation criterion instead of submitting a generic corporate proposal.

Tender Review and Contract Award

The Global Fund’s procurement framework includes controls before contracts are awarded.

Its Procurement Policy states that procurement contracts are subject to a mandatory review process prior to award to confirm compliance with applicable policies and procurement rules. No award may be made before that review is completed.

This reflects the organization’s emphasis on transparency, accountability and procurement integrity.

Are These Opportunities Based in Geneva?

Many opportunities published through this particular portal primarily involve supplying goods or services to the Global Fund Secretariat in Geneva, Switzerland.

However, this does not necessarily mean every consultant must permanently reside in Switzerland.

Assignment location, travel requirements, remote-working arrangements and geographical eligibility can differ substantially from one tender to another.

Applicants should therefore consult the individual Terms of Reference rather than assuming an opportunity is either remote or Geneva-based.

Can International Applicants Apply?

The Global Fund Business & Consultancy Opportunities page does not establish one universal nationality restriction covering all tenders.

It states that open tenders are available for prospective suppliers to review and consider. The Supplier Code also covers a broad range of bidders, suppliers, consultants, contractors, organizations and representatives.

However, international eligibility must be determined tender by tender.

A specific procurement may impose requirements relating to:

  • Country registration
  • Geographic presence
  • Local expertise
  • Language
  • Tax registration
  • Professional licensing
  • Experience in certain regions
  • Ability to travel
  • Manufacturer authorization
  • Product regulatory approval

Applicants should therefore never interpret the general procurement page as guaranteeing eligibility for every nationality in every procurement.

Are There Opportunities for Applicants From Africa, Asia, Europe and Other Regions?

Potentially, yes, depending on the specific tender.

The Global Fund operates globally, and its procurement ecosystem includes international companies, consultants, manufacturers and service providers. But there is no blanket statement on the Business & Consultancy Opportunities page saying every tender is universally open to every country.

Applicants from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, Latin America, the Caribbean, the Middle East and Oceania should check the nationality, registration and location provisions of each individual procurement notice.

Application Deadline

There is no single overall deadline for Global Fund Business & Consultancy Opportunities.

This is an ongoing procurement portal.

Each open tender has its own closing date and submission time, which are stated within the individual solicitation documentation. The official page specifically directs applicants to the individual tender for submission instructions and contact information.

Applicants should therefore:

  1. Open the current tender list.
  2. Identify the relevant opportunity.
  3. Check its exact closing date.
  4. Note the applicable time zone.
  5. Submit the complete proposal before the stated deadline.

Late submissions may not be accepted under tender-specific rules.

Important Difference Between Global Fund Tenders and Global Fund Jobs

Applicants should understand that this procurement portal is not the Global Fund’s ordinary employment vacancies page.

The organization maintains a separate recruitment system for staff vacancies. Its careers page specifically explains that consulting opportunities for consultants and consultancy firms are listed under Business & Consultancy Opportunities.

Therefore:

Permanent or temporary employment: Check Global Fund Careers.

Consultancy contracts, supplier opportunities and tenders: Check Business & Consultancy Opportunities.

This distinction is particularly important for applicants preparing CVs or proposals.

Why Consider Global Fund Business Opportunities?

Working with the Global Fund can provide experienced consultants and organizations with an opportunity to contribute specialized expertise to one of the world’s major global health financing institutions.

Potential benefits include:

  • Participation in international health initiatives
  • Exposure to complex global programs
  • Opportunities to work with international stakeholders
  • Experience with major institutional procurement systems
  • Potential long-term professional relationships
  • Opportunities for specialist consulting firms
  • Participation in health-product and supply-chain initiatives
  • Work contributing indirectly to the fight against HIV, tuberculosis and malaria

However, applicants should approach these opportunities as formal competitive procurements rather than guaranteed contracts.

Tips for Prospective Applicants

Before submitting a Global Fund tender, applicants should:

  1. Read the complete Terms of Reference or technical specifications.
  2. Confirm that all mandatory eligibility criteria can be satisfied.
  3. Read the Procurement Policy.
  4. Review the Supplier Code of Conduct.
  5. Examine the applicable Terms and Conditions.
  6. Prepare a proposal specifically tailored to the tender.
  7. Demonstrate relevant experience with evidence.
  8. Provide qualified personnel where required.
  9. Address every evaluation criterion.
  10. Ensure pricing is complete and commercially realistic.
  11. Disclose potential conflicts where required.
  12. Avoid unsupported claims about organizational capacity.
  13. Confirm the deadline and applicable time zone.
  14. Submit through the method specified in the tender.
  15. Retain copies of all documents submitted.

Important Warning for Applicants

Applicants should use only official Global Fund procurement channels and verify all tender information against the official website.

A legitimate procurement process should include formal documentation defining the required goods or services, submission requirements and applicable conditions.

Prospective bidders should also remember that winning a Global Fund contract does not provide unrestricted permission to use the organization’s name or logo for advertising purposes.

Conclusion

The Global Fund Business & Consultancy Opportunities platform provides an important route for qualified consultants, businesses, manufacturers, contractors and professional service providers seeking to work with an internationally recognized global health financing organization.

Unlike a conventional job board, the platform operates as an ongoing competitive procurement system, with individual tenders covering different goods, consulting assignments and specialized services.

The Global Fund emphasizes transparency, effective competition, integrity, sustainability and value for money throughout its procurement activities. Applicants should therefore expect rigorous technical, ethical and contractual standards.

There is no universal application deadline. Each opportunity has its own closing date, technical requirements, financial requirements and submission procedure.

Prospective suppliers and consultants should regularly review the official portal, identify opportunities aligned with their expertise, carefully study all tender documentation and prepare compliant, evidence-based proposals.

Explore Current Global Fund Business & Consultancy Opportunities

For more global opportunities, click HERE.

item.content:encoded:
Applications are now open for the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Spring 2027 Internship Program, offering emerging professionals an opportunity to gain practical experience inside one of the largest departments of the U.S. federal government.

The Spring 2027 cohort will run from January 25 through April 30, 2027, with applications due by November 13, 2026. The program is an unpaid, in-person volunteer internship based in Washington, D.C. USDA does not provide housing or relocation assistance.

Unlike many internships that are limited to currently enrolled university students, USDA’s current Internship Program does not require applicants to be enrolled in school or to hold a college degree. According to USDA’s official FAQ, applicants must be U.S. citizens and at least 18 years old at the time of application. Candidates from a wide range of educational and professional backgrounds may therefore be considered.

The program provides participants with direct exposure to public service and federal government operations while allowing them to contribute to work related to agriculture, food systems, conservation, rural communities, communications, research, public policy, stakeholder engagement and other areas central to USDA’s mission.

About the USDA Internship Program

The U.S. Department of Agriculture describes its Internship Program as a public-service and leadership-development experience intended to introduce emerging leaders to USDA’s work and help prepare them for careers in public service, agriculture, science, policy and community development.

USDA’s mission reaches far beyond farming alone. The Department works across areas including:

  • Agriculture and agricultural markets
  • Food and nutrition
  • Food safety
  • Rural economic development
  • Natural-resource conservation
  • Forestry and environmental stewardship
  • Agricultural research
  • Data and economics
  • International agricultural trade
  • Communications
  • Public policy
  • Congressional relations
  • Civil rights
  • Community partnerships
  • Stakeholder engagement

Interns may therefore have opportunities to work in areas aligned with a broad range of academic interests, professional skills and career ambitions.

USDA states that interns may contribute to activities such as research, program operations, data analysis, communications, outreach and stakeholder engagement. Exact responsibilities depend on the mission area or staff office in which an intern is placed.

Spring 2027 USDA Internship Dates

The current application is specifically for the Spring 2027 cohort.

Program period: January 25, 2027 – April 30, 2027

Application deadline: November 13, 2026

USDA’s application information states that applicants should be available during the program period. The application form itself also allows candidates with limited availability to explain their circumstances, although applicants should expect the program to require substantial in-person participation.

Applicants should therefore carefully consider academic, employment, transportation and housing commitments before applying.

Is the USDA Spring 2027 Internship Paid?

No.

The current USDA Spring 2027 Internship Program is explicitly described as an unpaid volunteer internship. Applicants will not receive a salary from USDA through this program.

This distinction is important because USDA also operates other student employment initiatives, including Pathways opportunities, some of which may be paid. The internship advertised on the USDA page linked above, however, is the USDA Volunteer Internship Program and is unpaid.

USDA encourages applicants to explore whether their educational institutions or relevant nonprofit organizations can provide funding or academic support.

Applicants should also be aware that outside income, funding or housing assistance associated with the internship may require prior approval from USDA.

Housing and Relocation Assistance

USDA does not provide housing specifically for interns under this program.

Participants are responsible for finding and paying for their own accommodation for the duration of the internship.

USDA also states on the Spring 2027 application page that the program provides no housing or relocation assistance.

Candidates who do not already live within commuting distance of Washington, D.C., should therefore calculate expected costs before accepting an internship, including:

  • Housing
  • Transportation
  • Meals
  • Local commuting
  • Relocation expenses
  • Personal living expenses

Because the position is unpaid, financial planning will be particularly important for applicants relocating to Washington.

Internship Location: Washington, D.C.

The USDA Internship Program is conducted in person in Washington, D.C.

Interns are expected to work onsite at USDA’s Whitten Building, where they participate directly in departmental operations and interact with USDA personnel.

USDA specifically states that remote participation is not available for this program.

Applicants should therefore not apply on the assumption that they will be permitted to complete the internship remotely from another U.S. state or another country.

Expected Internship Schedule and Working Hours

Most USDA internships under this program operate on a Monday-to-Friday schedule, typically within approximately 9:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m.

Some flexibility may be available for interns who have academic or other program requirements.

USDA states that interns considered full-time are generally expected to work the equivalent of approximately 4.5 days per week, although limited adjustments may be permitted where appropriate.

Applicants should therefore view the opportunity as a substantial professional commitment rather than a few-hours-per-week volunteer placement.

What Will USDA Interns Do?

Specific duties will depend heavily on the intern’s assigned mission area or staff office.

USDA identifies potential internship activities including:

  • Conducting research
  • Supporting program operations
  • Analyzing data
  • Drafting communications
  • Assisting with outreach activities
  • Supporting stakeholder engagement
  • Developing briefing materials
  • Supporting meetings and events
  • Conducting policy-related research
  • Helping coordinate projects
  • Participating in departmental programming

This structure allows interns to gain practical experience while contributing to ongoing federal government activities.

Leadership and Professional Development

The program is not intended to consist solely of administrative assignments.

USDA describes it as a leadership-development and public-service experience designed to help young and emerging professionals better understand federal service.

Interns participate in department-wide programming, including lunch-and-learn sessions featuring USDA leaders and subject-matter experts.

Through these activities, interns may gain exposure to:

  • Federal decision-making
  • Government leadership
  • Agriculture and food policy
  • Public administration
  • Interagency operations
  • Stakeholder engagement
  • Professional networking
  • Career development
  • Public-service culture

USDA Mission Areas and Offices Available to Applicants

As part of the application, candidates must list their top three preferred USDA Mission Areas or Staff Offices.

USDA’s official Office Opportunities document identifies a wide range of potential placement areas.

1. Farm Production and Conservation

Farm Production and Conservation (FPAC) serves as a major focal point for farmers, ranchers and other stewards of private agricultural and forest lands.

Its work includes programs related to:

  • Crop insurance
  • Agricultural conservation
  • Farm safety nets
  • Lending
  • Disaster programs
  • Risk mitigation for agricultural producers

This area may be particularly relevant for applicants interested in agricultural economics, environmental policy, farming systems, risk management or public administration.

2. Food and Nutrition Administration

The Food and Nutrition Administration focuses on reducing food insecurity and improving nutrition security in the United States.

Its work includes administration of federal domestic nutrition-assistance programs as well as science-based nutrition guidance, policy coordination and nutrition education.

This area may appeal to applicants interested in food security, nutrition, social policy, public health or program management.

3. Food Safety and Inspection Service

The Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) is USDA’s public-health agency responsible for helping ensure the safety of meat, poultry and egg products.

Its work includes food-safety oversight and implementation of federal laws governing meat, poultry, egg products and humane animal handling.

Students and professionals interested in food science, public health, veterinary science, regulatory policy or compliance may find this mission area particularly relevant.

4. Marketing and Regulatory Programs

Marketing and Regulatory Programs (MRP) supports domestic and international agricultural markets while protecting U.S. plant and animal health.

Its responsibilities include:

  • Agricultural marketing
  • Plant health
  • Animal health
  • Biotechnology regulation
  • Animal-welfare administration
  • Wildlife-damage management
  • Participation in national and international standards development

5. Research, Education and Economics

The Research, Education and Economics (REE) mission area supports research, analysis and education related to a safe, competitive and sustainable U.S. food and agricultural system.

Its work also addresses communities, families and young people.

Applicants interested in science, statistics, economics, research, data analysis or education may find REE especially relevant.

6. Rural Development

USDA Rural Development supports rural communities through loans, grants and loan-guarantee programs.

Its work includes investments relating to:

  • High-speed internet
  • Electricity
  • Transportation infrastructure
  • Businesses
  • Healthcare
  • Education
  • Housing
  • Community facilities

This placement could be highly relevant for students of economics, finance, infrastructure, public policy, community development or business administration.

7. Trade and Foreign Agricultural Affairs

Trade and Foreign Agricultural Affairs (TFAA) works to expand international opportunities for American farmers and ranchers.

Its responsibilities include international agricultural trade policy, market intelligence, trade promotion and export development.

USDA’s Foreign Agricultural Service maintains a global network covering numerous countries, while the U.S. Codex Office coordinates American participation in international food-standard setting.

This area may be particularly attractive to applicants interested in international relations, economics, trade, diplomacy, agriculture or global food policy.

8. Natural Resources and Environment

The Natural Resources and Environment (NRE) mission area focuses on maintaining the health, diversity and productivity of U.S. forests and grasslands.

It works with states, tribes and communities across the country to steward natural resources.

Applicants with interests in environmental studies, forestry, climate policy, conservation, sustainability or natural-resource management may consider this placement.

USDA Staff Offices Offering Internship Exposure

Applicants can also express preferences for USDA staff offices.

Office of the Secretary

The Office of the Secretary provides leadership and strategic direction across USDA.

Interns may support:

  • High-level policy coordination
  • Research
  • Briefing materials
  • Departmental decision-making
  • Senior leadership meetings
  • Major events

This placement provides particularly close exposure to senior-level federal policy and executive decision-making.

White House Liaison Office

The White House Liaison Office connects USDA with the Executive Office of the President.

Its responsibilities include personnel matters, political appointments, leadership onboarding and coordination with the White House.

Interns may assist with research, personnel processes, organizational analysis, briefings and leadership engagements.

Office of Communications

The Office of Communications manages public information and strategic communication across USDA.

Internship work may involve:

  • Writing and editing
  • Press support
  • Briefing materials
  • Digital content
  • Media monitoring
  • Event support
  • Visual storytelling
  • Strategic messaging

It may be particularly suitable for applicants interested in journalism, public relations, communications, digital media or public affairs.

Office of Congressional Relations

The Office of Congressional Relations acts as USDA’s main liaison with the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate.

Interns may gain experience in:

  • Legislative research
  • Tracking congressional hearings
  • Monitoring legislation
  • Preparing background materials
  • Congressional communications
  • Supporting departmental engagements with lawmakers

Office of the Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights

The Office of the Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights (OASCR) leads USDA’s work relating to civil-rights compliance and equal treatment.

Potential intern activities include:

  • Civil-rights policy research
  • Data analysis
  • Training-material preparation
  • Outreach
  • Compliance-related work

Office of Partnerships and Public Engagement

The Office of Partnerships and Public Engagement (OPPE) works with rural and underserved communities and helps connect stakeholders with USDA programs and resources.

Interns may assist with:

Who Can Apply?

One of the distinctive features of the current USDA internship is its relatively broad educational eligibility.

According to USDA:

  • Applicants must be at least 18 years old.
  • Applicants must be U.S. citizens.
  • Applicants do not need to be currently enrolled in school.
  • Applicants do not need to hold a college degree.
  • People from a wide range of educational and professional backgrounds may apply.

The online application provides education-status options including:

  • Currently enrolled in high school
  • Currently enrolled in college or university
  • Recently graduated
  • Not currently enrolled in school

This confirms that the program is not restricted solely to university students.

Does an Applicant Need a Specific Major?

No specific academic major is identified as a universal requirement for the program.

The application nevertheless asks candidates to identify their major or field of study, where applicable. Applicants who are not currently enrolled may provide their most recent field of study or indicate that the question is not applicable.

Given USDA’s broad responsibilities, potentially relevant backgrounds include—but are not limited to:

  • Agriculture

Applicants should choose office preferences that align logically with their interests, abilities and professional goals.

Is a Minimum GPA Required?

The application asks candidates to provide a GPA, but USDA marks the GPA field as optional.

The current program page therefore does not establish a universal minimum GPA requirement for the Spring 2027 Volunteer Internship Program.

USDA Internship Application Requirements

The application must be submitted through USDA’s official online portal.

Hard-copy applications sent by mail are not accepted.

Applicants will need to complete several sections.

Section 1: Personal Information

Applicants provide details including:

  • Full name
  • Street address
  • City, state and ZIP code
  • Telephone number
  • Email address

Section 2: Education

Applicants indicate their education status and provide applicable details such as:

  • Current school or university
  • Major or field of study
  • Expected graduation date
  • GPA, if they choose to provide it

Section 3: Spring 2027 Availability

Applicants must indicate whether they are available for the full Spring 2027 semester or have limited availability.

Candidates selecting limited availability must provide an explanation.

Section 4: Statement of Interest

The application requires substantive written responses addressing several topics.

Applicants are asked to explain:

  1. Why they are interested in an internship with USDA.
  2. What skills and experiences they could bring to USDA.
  3. Which issues affecting agriculture, food systems, conservation or rural communities they want to learn more about and why.
  4. What public service means to them and how they have demonstrated commitment to their community.
  5. A personal accomplishment they are proud of and how it shaped their perspective on success.

The application also asks whether applicants have previously volunteered or worked for a:

  • Political campaign
  • Elected official
  • Government official

Applicants answering yes are asked to describe their role and the relevant campaign, office or official as well as the year or years involved.

Importantly, USDA states separately that political preference is not used as a deciding factor in internship application review.

Section 5: Office Preferences

Candidates must identify their top three USDA Mission Areas or Staff Offices where they would prefer to intern.

Applicants should research these offices before selecting preferences because their choices can help communicate their career interests and indicate where their skills may best fit USDA’s needs.

Section 6: References

Applicants must provide at least two references who can discuss their:

  • Qualifications
  • Character
  • Work ethic
  • Commitment to public service

USDA suggests potential references such as:

  • Professors
  • Supervisors
  • Mentors
  • Community leaders

Applicants should provide complete contact information for each reference.

Recommendation letters are optional and may be uploaded as PDF documents if applicants wish to include them.

All required reference information must be submitted by the application deadline.

USDA notes that applications are reviewed on a rolling basis, which makes early submission advisable.

Resume Requirement

Applicants must upload a resume.

The application portal currently accepts:

  • PDF
  • DOC
  • DOCX

The maximum upload size shown on the application form is 20 MB.

Candidates should tailor their resume to demonstrate relevant experience rather than using a generic resume whenever possible.

Useful information may include:

  • Education

  • Leadership activities
  • Community involvement

  • Public-service activities
  • Relevant technical skills
  • Communication skills
  • Data or analytical experience
  • Policy experience
